definition: The natural logarithm of a token's predicted probability, commonly used instead of raw probability for numerical stability and easier aggregation across a sequence.
details: Log probabilities are summed rather than multiplied across a sequence to compute overall sequence likelihood, avoiding the numerical underflow that would occur when multiplying many small probabilities together.

explainer.lead: Log probability is the natural logarithm of a token's predicted probability, used in place of raw probability. It matters because it keeps very small likelihoods representable and makes sequence scores easy to combine.

tiers.eli5: Instead of saying a chance is one in a million, you write down how many zeroes it has, which is easier to add up across a long sentence.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers sum log probabilities across a sequence to score or compare candidate outputs, such as ranking generated text. A pitfall is forgetting that summed scores favour shorter or longer sequences unless normalised by length.
tiers.paperLevel: For a token with predicted probability p, the log probability is the natural logarithm of p; sequence likelihood is the sum of token log probabilities rather than their product, avoiding numerical underflow from multiplying many small probabilities.

explainer.example: A system compares two candidate completions of five and eight tokens; it sums each token's log probability to compare them and divides by length so the longer one is not unfairly penalised.
